catalog_quote: 3.2 There are four emic micro-segments, based on the contrastive placement of accent. (1) Monosyllabic micro-segments have an accent: "taal 'earth', "aat 'water', "et 'beans', "ca 'with'. (2) Most polysyllabic micro-segments receive penultimate accent: "taagat 'man', "yoliik 'he was born', na"nakat 'mushroom', či"kawak 'he's strong', čiči"pika 'it drips'. The basic accent pattern of micro-segments is retained in the compounding processes. (3) An antepenultimate accent pattern occurs when any of the following syllables (post-clitics) is suffixed to a polysyllabic micro-segment: -ti 'nominalizer', -sah 'just', -ok 'still', -ya 'now'. Although these four clitics manifest the features of micro-juncture and, therefore, should invoke the placement of penultimate stress, their occurrence results in a perturbation of accent placement, i.e., an antepenultimate accent pattern: "tepos 'metal', "teposti 'metal', "tepossah 'just metal'; "pajti 'medicine', "pahtiok 'it's still medicine'; "yahki 'he went', "yahkiya 'he's now gone'. (4) Another anomalous accent pattern, that of pre-antepenultimate accent occurs when two such post-clitics are suffixed to a polysyllabic micro-segment: "tepos 'metal', "teposti 'metal', "tepostisah 'it's just metal' ... [fn. 26, p. 32:] In grammatical terms, any morpheme of two or more syllables has penultimate stress and that stress will be retained in compounding. A free morpheme of one syllable has stress. Bound morphemes of one syllable do not have stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Highland Puebla Nahuatl (high1278, azz) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had one title-keyword item, Robinson 1969 'Puebla (Sierra) Nahuat prosodies' (SIL Publications in Linguistics 22, pp. 15-32), which was already downloaded (Internet Archive copy of the sil.org PDF, scanned, scanned) under by an earlier reading; I re-read the scanned and verified the deciding passage against the page image. It is a first-hand phonology of the Zacapoaxtla (Xalacapan) dialect and states that word-level accent (stress plus raised pitch) is penultimate in polysyllables, retained under compounding, with antepenultimate accent when one of four post-clitics (-ti, -sah, -ok, -ya) is suffixed and pre-antepenultimate when two are stacked; monosyllabic free morphemes are stressed, bound monosyllables are not (sec. 3.2 p. 19; fn. 26 p. 32). Vowel length is independent of stress. The same author's Aztec Studies II (1970, p. 1-2, held by the project) summarizes 'primary stress is on the penultimate syllable of the word - except for a few patterns of ultimate and antepenultimate placement', and fn. 3 quotes McQuown 1942 on the Nauzontla variety (mostly penultimate, a good number antepenultimate, a few final). This is a suitable deciding source for a new catalog record: penultimate, quantity-insensitive, clitic-extrametrical. Not obtained (already noted): Key & Key 1953 IJAL 19:53-56 (paywalled, DOI page could not be reached by automated download), Key & Ritchie de Key 1953 vocabulary (sil.org could not be reached by automated download), Robinson 1966 Hartford dissertation (archive.org lending-restricted), McQuown 1942, Troiani 1979 -- none is expected to outrank Robinson 1969, so acquisition priority is low. updated with a dated search line.

The basic accent pattern of micro-segments is retained in the compounding processes[f…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word (micro-segment) accent = stress plus raised pitch, predictable: monosyllables are accented; polysyllabic words are accented on the penult. The post-clitics -ti (nominalizer/absolutive), -sah 'just', -ok 'still', -ya 'now' do not shift the accent, so forms with one such clitic surface with antepenultimate accent and with two clitics pre-antepenultimate (tépos, téposti, tépostisah); all other suffixation re-places accent on the new penult. Any morpheme of two or more syllables has penultimate stress, retained (as tertiary) in compounds.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees of accent by prosodic domain: primary accent on the nucleus of the macro-segment (clause), secondary accent + high pitch on the nucleus (final micro-segment, penultimate syllable) of the meso-segment (phonological phrase ~ grammatical word), tertiary accent on the penult of non-final micro-segments (roots) inside compounds/phrases. Free monosyllabic morphemes bear stress; bound monosyllables do not (fn. 26).
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate (and pre-antepenultimate) accent with the enclitics -ti, -sah, -ok, -ya (one or two stacked); a small set of high-pitched particles (nohón 'that', aačáa 'perhaps', akcáa 'someone') whose pitch is unaffected by stress; Robinson 1970 also mentions 'a few patterns of ultimate.. placement'. McQuown 1942 (Nauzontla, quoted fn. 3) likewise reports mostly penultimate with a good number of antepenultimate and a few final-stressed forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of the basic rule is the micro-segment (phonological word, 1-6 syllables, never in isolation); the grammatical word with ordinary suffixes = meso-segment, whose nucleus keeps penultimate secondary accent; examples are from texts, conversation and paradigms gathered around Zacapoaxtla (Xalacapan).
new_statements.identity_note: Robinson 1969/1970 describe 'Sierra Nahuat' (SN) from Xalacapan, municipio of Zacapoaxtla, Puebla (fieldwork 1958-62); fn. 5 defines the dialect as the area bounded by Teziutlan, Zautla, Tetela de Ocampo and Cuetzalan with Zacapoaxtla at its centre = Glottolog high1278 / ISO azz (Highland Puebla / Sierra Puebla Nahuatl). Key & Key 1953 describe the same Zacapoaxtla variety. McQuown 1942 (quoted second-hand) is Nauzontla, same dialect area; Troiani 1979 is San Miguel Tzinacapan (Cuetzalan), also within azz.

new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate word stress (stress-cum-high-pitch on the penult of the stem/word), quantity-insensitive (long vowels do not attract stress), with morphologically conditioned antepenultimate and pre-antepenultimate stress when the extrametrical post-clitics -ti, -sah, -ok, -ya are added (one clitic -> antepenult, two -> pre-antepenult); monosyllabic free words stressed. Coding candidate: penultimate, fixed/morphological, clitic-extrametrical; not weight-sensitive.

new_statements.quote: 8. El acento prosódico primario ocurre en la penúltima sílaba de toda palabra polisílaba. Las palabras monosilábicas tienen su acento particular. Dos sílabas comunes que parecen quebrantar esta regla son: -ti, un enclítico que entra en la formación de substantivos, que no cambia el acento cuando va como sufijo de la raíz, y -tzin, sufijo honorífico, de encarecimiento o diminutivo, que contiene una vocal larga que se oye como más prominente que el acento efectivo que se haya en la sílaba anterior.
new_statements.translation: 8. Primary prosodic accent falls on the penultimate syllable of every polysyllabic word. Monosyllabic words have their own accent. Two common syllables that seem to break this rule are: -ti, an enclitic that enters into the formation of nouns, which does not change the accent when it is suffixed to the root, and -tzin, an honorific, endearing or diminutive suffix, which contains a long vowel that is heard as more prominent than the actual accent on the preceding syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same penultimate placement as the catalog record (penultimate stress) and as Robinson 1969 sec. 3.2; adds the earliest (1953) statement for this variety, the same -ti clitic-extrametricality already noted from Robinson 1969 fn. 26, and a new note on -tzin (long-vowel prominence competing with the accent). Explicitly about the Zacapoaxtla dialect (p. v: 'el dialecto que se habla alrededor del municipio de Zacapoaxtla, Puebla'), i.e. high1278.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of every polysyllabic word; monosyllables are stressed. The noun-forming enclitic -ti is stress-neutral (the stem keeps its penult accent, so the surface word ends up antepenult-stressed), and the honorific/diminutive suffix -tzin has a long vowel that is perceived as more prominent than the preceding, actually-accented syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Two apparent exceptions: the noun enclitic -ti (does not shift the accent from the root, so the accent surfaces on the antepenult) and the suffix -tzin (long vowel perceived as more prominent than the accented penult of the stem). The vocabulary itself does not mark stress in entries; long vowels are underlined.
new_statements.identity_note: Key & Key 1953 describes the Nahuat of the municipio of Zacapoaxtla, Puebla, and says it serves for many towns of the northern Sierra de Puebla; this is the variety Glottolog high1278 (Highland Puebla Nahuatl, ISO azz) covers, the same one Robinson 1969/1970 describe. The archive.org item for work 0 is confirmed to be the 1966 Hartford thesis on Zacapoaxtla Nahuat (MARC subject 'Aztec language - Dialects - Zacapoaxtla').

new_statements.quote: There are three emic stresses: primary, secondary, and weak. Placement of primary stress is on the penultimate syllable of the word - except for a few patterns of ultimate and antepenultimate placement. Only non-penultimate stress is marked in Nahuat word examples in this grammar. A word is defined phonologically as ending with the syllable which follows the primary stress. Secondary stress and weak stress, as well as the phonological units of syllable, phonological-word, phonological-phrase, phonological-clause, and phonological-sentences are not germane to this grammar; their definition can be found in the study referred to above.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author, same analysis as the catalog record (Robinson 1969 sec. 3.2: penultimate accent on polysyllabic micro-segments, antepenultimate with enclitics) and as Key & Key 1953 rule 8 (penultimate). The 1966/1970 text is a summary that explicitly defers to the prosodies study; it adds the word-domain definition (word ends with the post-tonic syllable) and names three stress degrees. No open copy of the 1966 typescript itself exists; its content on stress is available through this published edition.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate syllable; a few (unspecified here) patterns have ultimate or antepenultimate stress, and only those non-penultimate cases are marked in the grammar's examples; the phonological word is defined as ending one syllable after the primary stress. The full prosodic analysis is deferred to 'Sierra Nahuat Prosodies' (= Robinson 1969, the catalog source). Sec. 1.4 Morphophonemics (pp. 16-21, scanned checked) says nothing further about stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees named (primary, secondary, weak) but secondary and weak stress are explicitly left undescribed here ('not germane to this grammar'); referred to Sierra Nahuat Prosodies (Robinson 1969).
new_statements.exceptions: 'a few patterns of ultimate and antepenultimate placement' (not enumerated in sec. 1.1; non-penultimate stress is marked on examples through the grammar). Robinson 1969 (catalog source) attributes antepenultimate/pre-antepenultimate accent to the enclitics -ti, -sah, -ok, -ya.
new_statements.identity_note: Sierra Nahuat = the Nahuat (t-dialect) spoken within about 20 miles of Zacapoaxtla, Sierra Norte de Puebla (author resident in Xalacapan, fieldwork 1958-1964); the preface excludes detailed coverage of Cuetzalan and Chignahuapan variation. Glottocode high1278 Highland Puebla Nahuatl, ISO azz.

Sec. 3.2 (p.19): monosyllabic micro-segments (phonological words) are accented; most polysyllabic ones receive penultimate accent; antepenultimate accent arises when post-clitics -ti, -sah, -ok, -ya are suffixed (teposti, tepossah), pre-antepenultimate with two such clitics (tepostisah).
